title: A Survey on Bias and Fairness in Machine Learning

reading.body:
A 2019 survey that maps where bias enters machine learning and how researchers define fairness has become the field's standard reference, with 6,373 citations.

The pattern is consolidation. Before this survey, bias sources and fairness definitions were scattered across papers with incompatible vocabularies. The survey gathered real cases of unfair outcomes, sorted the reasons bias enters systems, and organized competing definitions of fairness into one structure. The citation count indicates the field adopted it as common ground.

For AI specifically, the survey matters because it is a prerequisite for testing rather than a test itself. An audit needs a taxonomy of bias sources and a set of fairness definitions before it can measure anything. The survey supplies both, which is why it is cited far more than any single fairness metric or debiasing method. It describes the problem space, not a solution.

The data does not say which bias sources or fairness definitions the survey identifies, how they relate, or whether any have held up since 2019. It records a DOI, a journal, an author list, a year, and a citation count. It also does not connect bias or fairness to compute, buildings, or power, and nothing here should be read as doing so.

explain_beginner: This survey looks at how artificial intelligence can treat people unfairly. It gathers examples from real uses where such unfairness appeared. It sorts the reasons bias can enter AI systems. It also organizes the different ways researchers define fairness, so people can compare ideas. The paper reviews many areas of AI and describes unfair results researchers found and attempts to fix them. It says more work is needed. This matters because AI often helps make important choices, so unfair treatment can harm groups. The survey gives a shared starting point for spotting and discussing bias.
explain_business: This survey explains that AI systems can make important decisions and may treat groups unfairly. It gathers real cases where bias appeared, identifies where bias can enter, and organizes the ways fairness is defined. It also reviews how different AI areas have shown unfair results and what researchers tried. For an executive, the practical message is that fairness needs attention during design and engineering. The paper provides a shared vocabulary and map of bias sources, which can guide how organizations discuss and review fairness. It also shows the field still lacks complete solutions, so more work is needed.
explain_practitioner: This 2019 survey by Mehrabi and colleagues reviews bias and fairness in machine learning. It collects real applications where bias has appeared and lists where bias can come from. It builds a taxonomy of how fairness is defined proposed by machine learning researchers. It then examines several AI domains and subdomains, reporting unfair outcomes seen in leading methods and approaches used to address them. The main contribution is a structured map of bias sources and fairness concepts, plus a review of problems in specific domains and fixes. It notes that many open problems remain. For engineers, it offers a reference for framing audits and comparing fairness choices before testing.
